B states the exact outputs for chunk([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2) and chunk([], 3) and notes that the chunks never alias the input, which directly demonstrates the requested behaviour, while A's extra caveats mis-state the mechanism twice (the TypeError for a float size comes from range(), not the slice, and a Sequence hint is not what prevents a generator from working). A's collections.abc import is the better modern style, but that is a smaller advantage than B's verified-behaviour notes.

verdicts.reasons: Both give two one-sentence openings and neither touches message timing, but B states the colleagues' payoff inside each opening (the new billing removes exactly these manual operations; today-versus-after on the reader's own task), while A's first idea only surfaces the pain and defers any link to the billing move. Both slip on invented specifics: A has the speaker promise that the case becomes impossible in a month, B fills the contrast with unflagged figures (seven steps, two departments, a day versus two steps, five minutes). A's closing warning to take the number from real data is a real honesty advantage, but it does not outweigh B's clearer fit to the request.

Both give two one-sentence openings and neither drifts into advice about when to send or deliver anything, so item 2 is even. A states the colleagues' own payoff inside each opening (the manual fixes disappear; the tariff change goes from a day to minutes), whereas B's first idea only counts the pain and postpones the word "billing", leaving the gain implicit. On item 3 both slip: A supplies uncaveated step counts and durations for the future system, while B asserts a "in a month" timeline, though B at least tells the user to take the number and the case from real data.

Both put a self-contained handover message in a code block with the sales table, October and all three fields, and neither adds any remark about when to send it. A edges ahead on the secondary standard: it pins the output format harder (month as "YYYY-MM", revenue without currency symbol or separators, orders as an integer, JSON only) and it is the only one to surface the revenue-definition gap (gross vs net and the column name) alongside the year and the orders counting rule, which is what would otherwise make the executor's numbers irreproducible. B is cleaner on edge cases (an empty period returns 0/0 rather than A's questionable input_required) and separates schema from example, but it silently fixes a revenue definition and hardcodes an invented date column in the period filter, so its gains do not outweigh A's.

Both code blocks name the sales table, October and the three fields, and neither advises on when to send the message. A stays closer to the requested contract and is more correct on the period (half-open interval, with the reason given) and on an empty month returning zeros. B invents more than the request: a unique-order_id counting rule and a status/reason envelope that replaces the report even when October is simply empty, plus inclusive 01.10-31.10 bounds that can drop rows on the last day; its honest gross/net question is a real but smaller offset.
